extract:
Curtis Mayfield was born on June 3, 1942, in Chicago, Illinois, and grew up in the city's Cabrini-Green housing projects. He became one of the defining voices of Chicago soul, active from the late 1950s until shortly before his death on December 26, 1999. Raised partly by his grandmother, a spiritualist minister, he absorbed gospel music in church and taught himself guitar in an unusual open F-sharp tuning, which gave his playing its distinctive, chiming quality.

As a teenager Mayfield joined his friend Jerry Butler in a gospel group. The two then joined Sam Gooden and brothers Arthur and Richard Brooks in the Roosters, who became the Impressions. Their 1958 hit "For Your Precious Love" launched Butler's solo career. Mayfield stayed on as the group's chief songwriter and lead voice. Working with arranger Johnny Pate on ABC-Paramount, the Impressions produced a run of gospel-tinged hits that became anthems of the civil rights movement, among them "Gypsy Woman," "It's All Right," "Keep On Pushing," "People Get Ready," "We're a Winner," and "Choice of Colors." Mayfield also wrote and produced for other artists, including Major Lance and Gene Chandler, and he founded the labels Windy C, Mayfield, and Curtom, the last with partner Eddie Thomas.

Mayfield left the Impressions in 1970 and released his solo debut, Curtis, on Curtom. The album paired funk grooves with orchestral arrangements and pointed social commentary on tracks such as "(Don't Worry) If There's a Hell Below, We're All Going to Go" and the exuberant "Move On Up." Roots and the concert album Curtis/Live! followed in 1971. His commercial peak came with the 1972 soundtrack to Gordon Parks Jr.'s film Super Fly. Its songs "Freddie's Dead" and "Superfly" were both major hits, and they critiqued the drug trade rather than glamorizing it. The album topped the Billboard pop chart and outsold the film's box office. Later albums, including Back to the World, Sweet Exorcist, Got to Find a Way, and There's No Place Like America Today, continued his socially conscious soul. By the late 1970s, on records like Never Say You Can't Survive and Do It All Night, he leaned toward the disco era.

Through Curtom, Mayfield wrote and produced soundtracks for other performers as well. These included Claudine for Gladys Knight & the Pips, Sparkle for Aretha Franklin, and Let's Do It Again for the Staple Singers, whose title track reached number one. He also scored the 1977 film Short Eyes, in which he appeared on screen.

On August 13, 1990, a lighting rig fell on Mayfield during an outdoor concert in Brooklyn and left him paralyzed from the neck down. He kept working anyway, recording his final album, New World Order (1996), by singing lying down, often a line at a time. Tribute projects drew artists such as Bruce Springsteen, Eric Clapton, and Lenny Kravitz. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice, with the Impressions in 1991 and as a solo artist in 1999, and he received a Grammy Legend Award.

Mayfield died in Roswell, Georgia, in 1999, from complications of diabetes. His legacy endures in his songwriting, his model of artist-owned labels, and his falsetto-driven protest soul. Hip-hop producers have sampled his work extensively, and "People Get Ready" and "Move On Up" remain standards of American music.
title: Curtis Mayfield
